title: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai Is David Dhawan's Farewell. The Reviews Say It Is Exactly What You Would Expect.
excerpt: Varun Dhawan, Mrunal Thakur, and Pooja Hegde deliver a throwback farce that critics call loud, colourful, and consistently watchable — if you have the appetite for '90s-style chaos.
body:
David Dhawan has made forty-six films. He says this one is his last.

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai opened in theatres on Friday, June 5, bringing together Varun Dhawan, Mrunal Thakur, and Pooja Hegde in a comedy that Dhawan describes as containing all the elements of a classic family entertainer: humour, confusion, music, and heartfelt moments. The advance booking data suggested a solid start — roughly 25,000 tickets were sold across PVRInox and Cinepolis before opening day, tracking ahead of Pati Patni Aur Woh Do and De De Pyaar De 2. The projection is an opening-day haul of around ₹8 crore.

The reviews have arrived, and they tell a consistent story. The film is an update of Dhawan's own 1996 hit Saajan Chale Sasural, a confession of allegiance to the formula that once made him and Govinda the rulers of the Hindi box office. Varun plays Jass, a wedding photographer who marries Bani (Thakur), splits up after five years over disagreements about having children, moves to London, falls for Preet (Hegde), and then discovers that both women are pregnant with his child simultaneously. The plot piles one absurd complication onto the next until nearly every female character in the film appears to be expecting.

## What the Critics Said

Filmfare gave it 3 out of 5, calling it an absurd comedy that tries to capture the magic of David Dhawan's '90s capers. Bollywood Hungama was more enthusiastic at 3.5 out of 5, saying the master director succeeds in his endeavour to make audiences sit back, relax, and have a gala time. Box Office Worldwide matched that rating, calling it a confident reminder of why Dhawan's brand of controlled chaos still has popular appeal.

Variety India was the outlier. Its review headline — "Varun Dhawan's Dated Throwback Comedy Should Have Stayed Locked Up in the Vault" — left no room for ambiguity. The review argued that neither intent from the filmmakers nor consent from the female characters played by Thakur and Hegde appears to matter much in the film, and that the script feels like a rough draft of a stand-up routine that was cancelled before opening night.

The middle ground is where most critics landed. The first half works better than the second. The London locations are picturesque. Chunari Chunari, the recreated Biwi No. 1 track, is a crowd-pleaser. Maniesh Paul is trapped in an eternal loop of sidekick duties. Logic does not apply — nor is it expected to.

## For Audiences Who Grew Up on Coolie No. 1

What makes the film culturally interesting is its relationship to time. David Dhawan's comedies of the 1990s — Coolie No. 1, Hero No. 1, Bade Miyan Chote Miyan — were the movies that played on loop in NRI households, the VHS tapes that circled through community gatherings in New Jersey, Southall, and Brampton. For a generation of diaspora kids, the Dhawan-Govinda pairing was background radiation, a constant hum of exaggerated chaos that somehow felt like home.

This film is a time capsule from that era, and it knows it. The question Filmfare posed — whether contemporary audiences still have an appetite for this style of comedy — is the only question that matters for its commercial fate.

Varun Dhawan, who has worked with his father in Judwaa 2 and Coolie No. 1 (2020), channels the energetic spirit of Govinda and Salman Khan's earlier performances while bringing what reviewers describe as a more mature screen presence. Mrunal Thakur provides emotional steadiness, and Pooja Hegde adds lively charm. Farhad Samji's dialogues reportedly land better in the second half than the first.

## The Verdict

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is not trying to be philosophical, socially relevant, or intellectually challenging. It is a clean, family-oriented entertainer — a species that multiple reviewers noted has become increasingly rare in today's Bollywood landscape. Whether that rarity creates demand or confirms irrelevance will be decided at the box office over the weekend.

For David Dhawan, who began his directorial career in 1988 and built an empire on the principle that audiences should leave theatres feeling lighter than when they walked in, the consensus is that his final film delivers enough spark to remain consistently watchable. It does not solve the limitations of its formula. It does not try to.

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is in theatres now.
